title: Ziervogel v. Royal Packing Co. (1949)
summary: The plaintiff could not rely on injuries outside the pleaded account without satisfying the applicable requirement for special damages.
notes:
This is a state decision and a fact-specific treatment of the injuries alleged. It does not establish that every bodily injury is special damage under Federal Rule 9(g).

The collision was at Vandeventer Avenue and North Market Street in St. Louis; the petition alleged injuries to her "neck, back, spine and nervous system"; the rule stated is that special damages must be pleaded or shown to be the necessary result of the injuries already alleged.

sections.Parties: Ziervogel sought damages from Royal Packing arising from a collision.
sections.Material Facts: The petition described injuries to the neck, back, and spine. At trial, evidence also concerned a shoulder injury and increased blood pressure. The plaintiff argued that the defendant or its insurer had information about those conditions, but the petition had not adequately identified them.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiff recovered a judgment after the trial court admitted evidence of the shoulder injury and increased blood pressure over objection. The Missouri Court of Appeals (St. Louis) reversed and remanded for a new trial on both liability and damages, holding that special damages must be specifically pleaded even though the defendant's insurer had actual notice of the conditions.
sections.Issue: Did allegations of the specified bodily injuries adequately encompass the additional shoulder and blood-pressure conditions?
sections.Holding: Not under the state pleading approach applied in this case. The additional matters required particular notice through the pleading.
sections.Reasoning: The court distinguished the injuries and consequences that ordinarily followed from the pleaded wrong from additional damage claims requiring specific identification. Information acquired elsewhere did not automatically expand the pleading. The chapter uses the decision to introduce the notice function of special-damage pleading and the potential importance of amendment.

learning.why: The plaintiff could not rely on injuries outside the pleaded account without satisfying the applicable requirement for special damages.

topics.cp-special-damages: The court treated the disputed injuries as requiring specific pleading under the applicable state approach.
topics.cp-amendment: Knowledge from outside the pleading did not substitute for an appropriate amendment.
topics.cp-frcp-9: The Missouri special-damages rule applied is the state counterpart of Rule 9(g), which requires special damages to be specifically stated.
topics.cp-pleading: The case is taught as the notice function of pleading: even actual knowledge by the defendant did not excuse failure to plead the injuries.
